tasks.prompt: Pressure loggers in an Ontario pressure zone show a sawtooth pattern: pressure builds slowly for 40 minutes, then drops sharply in 2 minutes, all night.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone supplied by a booster station with a small hydropneumatic tank and one duty pump on pressure control. Loggers record at 1 minute intervals at the station and at a high point.

evidence.label: Station logger shows pressure rising from 380 to 460 kPa over 40 minutes, then falling to 380 kPa in about 2 minutes, repeating all night.
The high point logger shows the same sawtooth, 30 kPa lower, in step with the station logger.
Pump run records show the duty pump starts exactly at each sharp pressure drop and stops at each peak.
The hydropneumatic tank is found waterlogged, with its air charge lost and the sight glass full.
Zone demand at night is low and steady, and no PRV or tank fill cycle operates on a 40 minute schedule.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The waterlogged hydropneumatic tank has lost its cushion, so small draws swing pressure widely and cycle the pump
A PRV in the zone is hunting on a 40 minute cycle
Customer demand cycles on a 40 minute industrial process
The pressure loggers share a common battery fault causing synchronised drift

inference.explanation: Both loggers agree, so logger fault is excluded. Pump starts align with the drops, and the tank is found waterlogged directly. No PRV or process operates on this cycle, and steady night demand cannot create a sawtooth that resets the moment the pump starts.

nextClue.prompt: Which fix best restores stable zone pressure?

options.label: Replace both pressure loggers with new units
Widen the pump pressure switch deadband without touching the tank
Restore the tank air charge or repair its bladder and verify the sawtooth flattens on the loggers

nextClue.explanation: Restoring the air cushion addresses the found fault. Widening the deadband would mask the symptom while the tank stays waterlogged and pump cycling continues.

clueText.nc-a: Both loggers agreed with each other and with pump starts, so they were reporting real pressure.
clueText.nc-b: A wider deadband leaves the waterlogged tank uncorrected and increases pressure swings at fixtures.
clueText.nc-c: After recharging, the overnight trace flattens to a 15 kPa band and pump starts fall from 18 to 3 per night.

tasks.prompt: A PRV station in Ontario holds its setpoint perfectly at low flow but downstream pressure climbs 120 kPa above setpoint every night when demand falls.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional single PRV station, setpoint 350 kPa, serving a residential zone. Upstream pressure is a steady 620 kPa. Loggers sit upstream and downstream.

evidence.label: Downstream pressure holds 350 kPa plus or minus 10 kPa from 06:00 to 23:00 daily.
Between 01:00 and 05:00 downstream pressure creeps up to 470 kPa, then returns to setpoint as morning demand starts.
Upstream pressure is steady at 620 kPa day and night, with no night rise.
With the PRV isolated and its downstream side drained in a test, downstream pressure rebuilds slowly with the PRV shut, showing seat leakage past the closed valve.
A second PRV station in the same system with the same setpoint holds 350 kPa all night.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Upstream pressure rises at night and overwhelms the PRV
The PRV main valve seat leaks at low flow, so downstream pressure creeps toward upstream pressure when demand cannot relieve it
The downstream logger reads high only at low temperature
Zone storage fills at night and backpressures the PRV station

inference.explanation: Upstream pressure never rises, so overwhelming is excluded. The paired station holds setpoint all night in the same temperatures, excluding logger and system effects. The isolation test shows pressure rebuilding past the shut valve, which is direct evidence of seat leakage.

nextClue.prompt: Which repair best addresses the night creep?

options.label: Overhaul the PRV main valve seat and pilot and retest downstream pressure at minimum night flow
Raise the setpoint to 470 kPa so night pressure matches the setting
Install a larger downstream pressure logger range

nextClue.explanation: Seat overhaul targets the demonstrated leak path. Raising the setpoint would legitimise excessive night pressure, and logger range does not change the pressure customers receive.

clueText.nc-a: After the seat overhaul, downstream pressure holds 348 to 355 kPa through the minimum flow hours.
clueText.nc-b: Raising the setpoint would expose the zone to the very overpressure the PRV exists to prevent.
clueText.nc-c: The logger correctly recorded pressures that customers and the isolation test confirmed.

tasks.prompt: Two parallel PRVs in an Ontario station were set identically. After maintenance on one valve, the station hunts and downstream pressure oscillates by 90 kPa.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional station with a small PRV for low flows and a large PRV for high flows, designed to stage at different setpoints. Both discharge to a common downstream header with a logger.

evidence.label: Before maintenance the station held downstream pressure within 15 kPa across the full flow range.
Maintenance records show the large PRV was reset to the same 350 kPa setpoint as the small PRV.
Downstream pressure now oscillates between 310 and 400 kPa, with both valves audibly opening and closing in turn.
When the large PRV is temporarily isolated, the small PRV alone holds a steady 350 kPa at current flows.
Upstream pressure and zone demand are steady during the oscillation periods.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Upstream pressure has become unstable since the maintenance
The downstream logger is oscillating due to a failing sensor
Identical setpoints make the parallel PRVs fight each other; staging requires the large valve set lower than the small valve
Zone demand now pulses in a way it never did before

inference.explanation: Isolating the large valve restores steady control, and upstream pressure and demand are steady, so neither supply nor demand explains the hunting. The maintenance record shows the staging offset was removed, which is the classic cause of parallel PRV fighting.

nextClue.prompt: Which setting change restores staged operation?

options.label: Set both PRVs 20 kPa higher to stiffen control
Reset the large PRV about 30 to 50 kPa below the small PRV so the small valve carries low flows alone
Lock the small PRV fully open and let the large valve control all flows

nextClue.explanation: A setpoint offset restores the designed staging: the small valve controls low flow, and the large valve opens only when pressure sags at high flow. Raising both together keeps them fighting.

clueText.nc-a: Raising both setpoints equally preserves the identical settings that cause the fighting.
clueText.nc-b: With the large PRV at 310 kPa and the small at 350 kPa, downstream pressure steadies within 12 kPa across the day.
clueText.nc-c: Locking the small valve open defeats low flow control, the duty it was sized for.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario elevated tank altitude valve fails to close, and the tank overflows on two consecutive nights despite normal pump controls.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional elevated tank filled by high lift pumps through an altitude valve that should close at the full level. Tank level and overflow are logged.

evidence.label: Tank level reaches the overflow level at 02:00 on two nights, with overflow confirmed by the site drain flow switch.
High lift pumps stop on their normal level signal at the set full level on both nights.
With pumps stopped, tank level continues to rise slowly for an hour, showing inflow continues past the altitude valve.
The altitude valve pilot line is found with a plugged strainer, and the valve responds sluggishly in a manual stroke test.
The tank level transmitter agrees with a manual tape reading within 0.1 m on both nights.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The high lift pumps are failing to stop at the full level
The level transmitter reads low, causing overfilling
Groundwater is entering the tank through a wall crack at night
The altitude valve is not closing fully because its pilot system is fouled, so inflow continues after the pumps stop

inference.explanation: Pump records show normal stops, and the transmitter agrees with the tape, excluding controls and sensing. Continued rise with pumps stopped isolates the altitude valve, and its fouled pilot strainer plus sluggish stroke confirm the mechanism.

nextClue.prompt: Which maintenance action best prevents the next overflow?

options.label: Lower the pump stop level by 1 m and leave the valve as is
Replace the level transmitter with a new model
Clean the pilot strainer, stroke test the altitude valve through full travel, and add the pilot to the inspection schedule

nextClue.explanation: Cleaning and stroke testing restores positive shutoff at the design level. Lowering the stop level wastes storage and still relies on a valve that does not close.

clueText.nc-a: A lower stop level reduces usable storage and leaves a valve that leaks past its seat uncorrected.
clueText.nc-b: The transmitter agreed with the manual tape, so replacement does not address the inflow past the valve.
clueText.nc-c: After cleaning, the valve closes fully in the stroke test and the next three fills stop at the set level with no overflow.

tasks.prompt: Pressure at the top of an Ontario hill zone is adequate all winter but fails on summer afternoons, while pressure at the bottom of the hill stays high.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional hill zone fed by a booster station at the bottom. Loggers at the station, mid hill, and hilltop run year round. Elevations differ by 45 m from station to hilltop.

evidence.label: Hilltop pressure falls to 140 kPa on summer afternoons but holds above 280 kPa on winter afternoons at similar station discharge pressure.
Station discharge pressure is the same 620 kPa in both seasons during the compared periods.
Summer afternoon zone demand is 2.5 times winter demand, driven by irrigation, per the station flow meter.
Mid hill pressure drops sit halfway between station and hilltop drops in both seasons.
A hydrant flow test at the hilltop in summer shows residual pressure falling steeply with flow, indicating high friction loss at peak flow.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Peak summer friction loss along the rising main consumes the head that winter flows leave available at the hilltop
The booster pumps lose performance every summer due to warm water
The hilltop logger reads low whenever temperature exceeds 25 C
The zone PRV opens in summer and dumps pressure to waste

inference.explanation: Station discharge pressure is identical in both seasons, so pump performance is not seasonal. Drops grade evenly with elevation and flow, and the hydrant test shows steep friction loss, which together identify friction at peak flow. A logger fault would not produce graded mid hill readings.

nextClue.prompt: Which capital or operating option best fits this diagnosis?

options.label: Evaluate looping or upsizing the rising main, since the limit is friction loss at peak flow, not station pressure
Replace the hilltop pressure logger
Raise station discharge pressure until hilltop complaints stop

nextClue.explanation: The diagnosis is a main capacity limit at peak flow, so the fix must reduce friction loss. Raising discharge pressure enough to offset it would overpressure the bottom of the hill, which already runs high.

clueText.nc-a: The hydraulic review confirms the rising main is the bottleneck and a looping main enters the capital plan.
clueText.nc-b: The hilltop logger agrees with graded mid hill readings and the hydrant test, so it is not faulty.
clueText.nc-c: Bottom of hill pressure is already high, so raising station pressure trades one problem for another.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario zone fed by two booster stations shows a persistent low pressure pocket exactly between the stations, worst when both stations run.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone with booster stations at its east and west ends feeding a looped grid. Loggers are placed on a grid across the zone for one month.

evidence.label: The low pressure pocket sits midway between the stations, with pressures 80 kPa below streets near either station.
The pocket worsens when both stations run together and eases when either station runs alone.
A normally open valve at the pocket, shown open on the plan, is found closed during the logger study.
Opening that valve in a supervised trial raises pocket pressures by 70 kPa with both stations running.
Station discharge pressures and pump curves both test normal throughout the study.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Both booster stations are undersized for the zone
The closed grid valve splits the zone so the midpoint is fed through long paths from both ends, doubling its friction loss
A large leak at the midpoint pulls pressure down
The midpoint loggers are all installed at a higher elevation than mapped

inference.explanation: Pumps test normal, and a leak would not improve the moment a grid valve opens. The trial opening restores 70 kPa directly, proving the grid configuration, not supply capacity, creates the pocket.

nextClue.prompt: Which record action locks in the trial result?

options.label: Schedule both stations for pump upgrades
Correct the valve status in the GIS and add the valve to the critical valve exercising list as normally open
Install a third booster station at the midpoint

nextClue.explanation: Recording the true status and exercising the valve protects the restored grid. The trial proved no new capacity is needed once the loop is whole.

clueText.nc-a: Station pumps tested normal and the valve trial fixed the pocket, so upgrades are not indicated.
clueText.nc-b: GIS is corrected the same week, and pocket pressures hold within 20 kPa of the zone average for the next month.
clueText.nc-c: A third station would mask a simple closed valve at far greater cost.

tasks.prompt: After a PRV station upgrade in Ontario, a zone that never had pressure complaints generates dozens, all for high pressure damage at night.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone. The upgrade replaced a direct acting PRV with a larger pilot operated PRV. Setpoint on the work order was 380 kPa. Complaints began the first night after the upgrade.

evidence.label: Night pressures at customer taps now reach 590 kPa, against 380 kPa before the upgrade.
The new PRV nameplate and pilot spring range cover 500 to 800 kPa, well above the 380 kPa setpoint on the work order.
Daytime pressures are near normal because demand holds the oversized valve in a controllable range.
The old PRV, still on site, has a spring range covering 200 to 450 kPa, which includes the setpoint.
Upstream pressure is unchanged at 640 kPa, and no other zone settings were altered.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Customers are reporting old damage that predates the upgrade
Upstream pressure rose the same night as the upgrade by coincidence
The replacement PRV pilot spring range cannot control down to the setpoint, so at low night flow the valve drifts toward upstream pressure
The setpoint was deliberately raised by the night operator

inference.explanation: Upstream pressure is unchanged and complaints began with the upgrade, excluding coincidence and old damage. The spring range physically excludes the setpoint, and the old valve range included it, which explains why control is lost only at low flow.

nextClue.prompt: Which corrective action best restores night control?

options.label: Raise the zone setpoint to 550 kPa to match the installed spring
Throttle a manual bypass valve each night to trim pressure
Fit a pilot spring in the correct range for 380 kPa and verify control at minimum night flow before returning the station to service

nextClue.explanation: Correct spring range restores automatic control at the design setpoint. Raising the setpoint accepts damaging pressure, and nightly manual throttling is not a control system.

clueText.nc-a: A 550 kPa setpoint would keep night pressure in the range that damaged customer fixtures.
clueText.nc-b: Manual nightly throttling depends on an operator visit and fails the first unattended night.
clueText.nc-c: With the correct spring fitted, night pressures hold 375 to 385 kPa at minimum flow on the verification log.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario pressure zone with an elevated tank shows its lowest pressures not at peak demand, but 30 minutes after the tank finishes filling.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone. High lift pumps fill the tank on a level cycle. Zone pressure and tank level are logged together at 5 minute intervals.

evidence.label: Zone pressure dips to its daily minimum about 30 minutes after each tank fill ends, then recovers slowly.
During fills, zone pressure is at its daily maximum, because the high lift pumps are running.
The dip coincides with the tank drain down period when the zone is supplied from the tank alone through a long 300 mm feed.
Tank outlet pressure logging shows a 90 kPa loss between the tank base and the zone grid at normal drain flows.
Customer demand during the dip periods is moderate, well below the afternoon peak that the zone handles without complaint.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The high lift pumps are undersized for the zone
The tank is too small and empties during the dip
A zone PRV closes during the dip periods
Friction loss in the long tank feed limits the zone whenever it depends on the tank alone

inference.explanation: Pressure is highest while pumps run, so pump capacity is not the limit, and the tank still holds water during dips. The measured 90 kPa loss on the tank feed at moderate flow explains why tank only supply underperforms pump supply.

nextClue.prompt: Which investigation best sizes the problem for a fix?

options.label: Run a controlled tank only drawdown test at several flows, logging tank base and grid pressures to build the feed loss curve
Replace the high lift pumps with larger units
Raise the tank overflow level to store more water

nextClue.explanation: A drawdown test quantifies feed loss against flow, which is the data needed to size a parallel feed or upsize. Larger pumps do not help a zone supplied from the tank, and more storage does not reduce friction loss.

clueText.nc-a: The drawdown test shows feed loss rising from 40 kPa at low flow to 130 kPa at peak drain flow, sizing the bottleneck.
clueText.nc-b: Pump supply periods already give the highest zone pressures, so pump size is not the constraint.
clueText.nc-c: A higher overflow adds volume but the dip occurs with water still in the tank, so volume is not the limit.

tasks.prompt: Pressure loggers at two ends of an Ontario zone disagree by 100 kPa at zero demand in the middle of the night, though the mains between them are looped and open.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone, looped grid, no PRVs between the two logger points, elevation difference surveyed at 2 m. Loggers were both calibrated the same week.

evidence.label: At 03:00 with near zero flow, Logger North reads 450 kPa and Logger South reads 350 kPa across an open looped grid.
Swapping the two loggers between sites swaps the readings: the high reading follows the North logger unit.
A calibrated test gauge at both sites reads 355 kPa and 352 kPa, matching Logger South.
Elevation difference between the sites is 2 m, worth about 20 kPa, not 100 kPa.
Daytime readings show the same fixed 100 kPa offset between the two logger units at all flows.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Logger North has a fixed calibration offset of about 100 kPa and its data should be excluded until recalibrated
A hidden PRV between the sites is cutting pressure by 100 kPa
A partially closed valve creates a 100 kPa loss even at zero flow
The elevation difference between the sites explains the gap

inference.explanation: At zero flow there can be no friction loss, and 2 m of elevation is worth only about 20 kPa. The offset follows the logger when swapped and the test gauge sides with Logger South, which isolates the instrument, not the network.

nextClue.prompt: Which data handling action is correct for the zone study?

options.label: Average the two loggers to get the true zone pressure
Flag and exclude Logger North data from the study, recalibrate it, and rely on Logger South and the test gauge points
Open more grid valves to equalise the two readings

nextClue.explanation: Excluding a proven faulty instrument protects the study conclusions. Averaging would bias every figure by 50 kPa, and valve work cannot fix an instrument offset.

clueText.nc-a: Averaging a faulty and a correct logger guarantees a wrong value at both sites.
clueText.nc-b: After recalibration, Logger North agrees with the test gauge within 5 kPa at both sites.
clueText.nc-c: The grid is already looped and open, and zero flow readings cannot be a friction effect.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario town creates a new pressure zone by closing boundary valves, and the new zone immediately shows fire flow failures at its far end.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional new zone split from a larger zone. The new zone is fed by one PRV station. Far end hydrants passed fire flow tests before the split.

evidence.label: Far end hydrant residual pressure at 60 L/s falls to 110 kPa, below the 140 kPa target, in tests after the split.
Before the split, the same hydrants were fed from two directions and passed at 180 kPa residual.
Static pressure in the new zone is normal at 400 kPa at all points, day and night.
The PRV station passes its full rated flow in a station test with only 30 kPa loss.
Opening one boundary valve to the old zone for a trial restores far end residual pressure to 175 kPa at the same test flow.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The PRV station is undersized for fire flow
Splitting the zone removed the second feed path, so far end fire flow now depends on one long path with high friction loss
The hydrants themselves deteriorated during the zone split
Static pressure in the new zone is too low for fire flow

inference.explanation: Static pressure is normal and the PRV passes full flow with small loss, excluding supply and setpoint. The trial reconnection restores residual pressure, proving the lost second path, not the hydrants, changed the result.

nextClue.prompt: Which design correction best restores fire protection in the new zone?

options.label: Raise the PRV setpoint by 100 kPa
Replace the far end hydrants with new units
Provide a second feed or loop into the new zone far end and retest fire flow at the critical hydrants

nextClue.explanation: A second path restores the hydraulics that passed before the split. Raising setpoint lifts static pressure but friction loss at fire flow would still consume it, and hydrants already proved sound when fed from two directions.

clueText.nc-a: Higher static pressure does not remove the friction loss measured at 60 L/s on the single path.
clueText.nc-b: The same hydrants passed at 175 kPa in the trial, so the hydrants are not the fault.
clueText.nc-c: A loop connection is designed for the far end, and the interim boundary valve is logged as normally open until it is built.

tasks.prompt: A rural Ontario pressure zone experiences pressure spikes to 900 kPa lasting seconds, several times a day, damaging a school plumbing system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone supplied by a booster station with two pumps alternating duty and a small subdivision at the zone edge. A transient logger records at high speed at the school.

evidence.label: High speed logging shows pressure rising from 450 to 900 kPa in under 2 seconds, then decaying over about 20 seconds.
Spikes align exactly with duty pump stop events in the station run log, on both pumps.
The station discharge check valves are a fast closing type, and no surge vessel or relief valve is fitted at the station.
Steady running pressures are normal, and the subdivision PRV holds its setpoint between spikes.
Spikes occur on dry and wet days alike and do not align with any customer or irrigation schedule.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The school pressure reducing valve is generating the spikes internally
Lightning induced pressure waves are entering the water main
Pump stoppage slams the check valves and sends a transient surge through the zone; surge protection at the station is missing
The transient logger is recording electrical noise as pressure

inference.explanation: Spikes align with pump stops on both pumps and decay like a hydraulic transient, and the station has fast closing checks with no surge device. The school PRV holds setpoint between events, and a logger artefact would not align with pump stops or damage plumbing.

nextClue.prompt: Which mitigation best addresses the mechanism?

options.label: Fit or restore surge control at the station, such as a surge vessel or relief valve, and review check valve closing speed
Replace the school plumbing with higher rated pipe
Lower the zone steady pressure by 50 kPa and leave surge control unchanged

nextClue.explanation: Surge control absorbs the transient at its source. Lower steady pressure still leaves a fast stoppage surge, and upgrading one customer does not protect the rest of the zone.

clueText.nc-a: A surge relief valve is fitted and the next month of high speed logging shows stops peaking at 540 kPa instead of 900 kPa.
clueText.nc-b: Higher rated school pipe treats one building while every other service still sees 900 kPa spikes.
clueText.nc-c: Steady pressure is already normal; the damage comes from the transient peak, not the baseline.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario zone altitude problem: a ground tank on a hill fills by gravity at night but its neighbourhood loses pressure every time the tank is taken offline for inspection.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional hill neighbourhood normally supplied through the ground tank, which floats on the system. A single feed main serves both the tank and the neighbourhood. Inspections take the tank offline for one week per year.

evidence.label: With the tank in service, neighbourhood pressures hold between 320 and 410 kPa across the day.
With the tank valved off, pressures fall below 180 kPa at morning and evening peaks, though the feed main pressure at the hill base stays at 430 kPa.
A flow test shows the single feed main loses 240 kPa at peak neighbourhood flow when the tank is offline.
With the tank online, peak flows are supplied locally from the tank, and feed main flows stay low with small losses.
No pumps serve the hill, and the pattern has repeated identically at three annual inspections.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The tank outlet valve leaks pressure away during inspection weeks
Neighbourhood demand triples during inspection weeks each year
The hill base pressure logger is faulty during inspections
The tank masks an undersized feed main: it supplies peaks locally, so the main only fails when the tank is offline

inference.explanation: Hill base pressure stays at 430 kPa offline, so supply to the hill is intact. The feed main loss of 240 kPa at peak flow with the tank offline explains the failure, and three identical repetitions exclude coincidence and seasonal demand claims.

nextClue.prompt: Which planning action follows from this finding?

options.label: Cancel future tank inspections to keep the tank online
Record the feed main as a capacity deficiency and programme its upsizing or a second feed, since growth will worsen the offline shortfall
Raise the hill base pressure with a temporary pump each inspection

nextClue.explanation: The finding is a latent capacity limit that inspections merely reveal. Cancelling inspections trades a known water quality and structural duty for hidden hydraulic risk, and temporary pumping repeats cost without fixing the main.

clueText.nc-a: Skipping inspections leaves tank condition unknown and does not change the undersized main.
clueText.nc-b: The feed main enters the capacity deficiency list with the flow test attached, and inspection planning now includes a demand advisory.
clueText.nc-c: Temporary pumping manages one week but leaves the deficiency unrecorded for growth planning.

tasks.prompt: A PRV in an Ontario station chatters loudly at morning peak, and downstream pressure pulses in time with the noise.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional PRV station serving a zone with a sharp 07:00 demand peak. The PRV is sized for fire flow. Normal zone flow is far below the valve rated minimum stable flow at peaks of valve travel near closed.

evidence.label: Chatter and pressure pulsing occur only between 06:30 and 08:00, when zone flow passes through a narrow band.
Valve position logging shows the main valve oscillating between 4 and 9 percent open during the chatter.
A smaller bypass PRV in the same station, currently valved out, is sized for the zone normal flow range.
Upstream pressure is steady, and downstream demand rises smoothly through the chatter band with no pulsing of its own.
The same station ran quietly for years when a former small PRV was in service in parallel.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The fire flow sized PRV is unstable near closed at normal flows; low flow control belongs on the small bypass PRV
Upstream pressure pulses are forcing the valve to chatter
The valve stem is bent and catches at one position
Air in the downstream main causes the pulsing

inference.explanation: Upstream pressure and demand are both smooth, excluding forcing from either side. Oscillation in a narrow low travel band, plus quiet history with a small valve in service, identifies oversizing instability rather than mechanical damage.

nextClue.prompt: Which station change restores quiet control?

options.label: Replace the large PRV with another valve of the same size
Add weight to the valve stem to damp the chatter
Return the small bypass PRV to service for normal flows and stage the large PRV to open only at high demand

nextClue.explanation: Staging a correctly sized small valve for normal flows is the designed remedy for low flow instability. A same size replacement would chatter identically, and stem weights are not a control solution.

clueText.nc-a: A same size valve has the same minimum stable flow, so the chatter band would remain.
clueText.nc-b: Damping the stem masks instability while seat wear from chatter continues.
clueText.nc-c: With the bypass PRV in service, morning peaks pass quietly and downstream pressure holds within 10 kPa.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario zone shows excellent pressures after a new booster station opens, except one crescent that gets worse than before the project.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional project: a new booster station replaced an old PRV feed. The crescent was formerly fed directly from the high pressure trunk. As built drawings differ from the design in one tie in location.

evidence.label: All zone loggers improve by 40 to 80 kPa after commissioning except the crescent, which falls by 60 kPa at peak.
The crescent is now fed through the new low zone instead of directly from the trunk, per the as built tie in location.
Trunk pressure at the old crescent feed point remains 580 kPa, and the old feed valve is closed and tagged.
Crescent demand and elevations are unchanged by the project.
Reopening the old trunk feed in a supervised trial restores crescent peak pressure to its former value.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The new booster station is undersized for the whole zone
The as built tie in moved the crescent into the lower pressure zone, removing the trunk feed it was designed around
The crescent developed a large leak during construction
Crescent homes added major new demand during the project

inference.explanation: Every other logger improved, so station capacity is not the issue. Demand is unchanged and the trial reconnection restores pressure exactly, proving the feed change, not a leak or growth, caused the local fall.

nextClue.prompt: Which project closeout action is correct?

options.label: Restore the crescent design feed or formally rezone it with a hydraulic check, and correct the as built record either way
Add the crescent to the leak survey list for the next quarter
Raise the new zone setpoint until the crescent recovers

nextClue.explanation: The cause is a feed configuration change, so the remedy is configurational and documentary. Raising the whole zone setpoint to fix one crescent would overpressure the rest of the zone.

clueText.nc-a: The crescent is reconnected to its design feed, its logger returns to former values, and the as built is corrected.
clueText.nc-b: No leak evidence exists, and the trial feed restoration already explains and fixes the fall.
clueText.nc-c: Zone wide setpoint increase would push already improved areas higher to solve a local tie in error.

tasks.prompt: Night pressure in an Ontario zone rises 80 kPa above daytime pressure, and the leakage team and the pressure team disagree about whether it is a fault.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone supplied by fixed speed high lift pumps against an elevated tank, with no PRV control. Loggers run at the low point and high point for a month.

evidence.label: Zone demand falls from 90 L/s by day to 18 L/s at night, per the plant flow record.
Low point pressure rises from 480 kPa by day to 560 kPa at night, while the tank cycles normally in its level band.
The rise is fully explained by reduced friction loss at low flow: a controlled test at 18 L/s by day reproduces 560 kPa.
No PRV, pump control change, or valve operation occurs at the times pressure rises.
Break frequency in the zone is highest in the lowest streets, where night pressure peaks.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A PRV is failing open at night and must be overhauled
The tank altitude valve is holding the zone at overflow pressure
The night rise is normal hydraulics for an uncontrolled zone, but it still drives night leakage and breaks at the low point
The low point logger drifts high at night

inference.explanation: The controlled daytime test at the same low flow reproduces the pressure, excluding any night specific fault, and there is no PRV in the supply to fail. Tank cycling is normal. The rise is real, measured, and hydraulically expected, yet still consequential for leakage and breaks.

nextClue.prompt: Which intervention best addresses the consequence without chasing a fault?

options.label: Overhaul the non existent PRV control on the zone feed
Consider pressure management, such as a PRV on the low subzone, evaluated against the measured night pressures and break locations
Recalibrate the low point logger until day and night agree

nextClue.explanation: Pressure management treats the measured condition and its break pattern. There is no PRV to overhaul on this feed, and forcing logger agreement would falsify good data.

clueText.nc-a: The zone feed has no PRV, so there is no valve whose overhaul could change the night rise.
clueText.nc-b: The low subzone is modelled for PRV control using the logger record, with breaks mapped to the highest night pressure streets.
clueText.nc-c: The logger reproduced its night value in a controlled daytime test, confirming it is accurate.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario booster station maintains zone pressure, but one pump station discharge logger shows pressure falling 50 kPa over a year while suction pressure is unchanged.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional station with two identical pumps. Discharge and suction loggers are calibrated together annually. Pump curves from commissioning are on file.

evidence.label: Duty pump discharge pressure at the standard test flow fell from 520 kPa to 470 kPa over 12 months, with suction steady at 210 kPa.
The standby pump, tested at the same flow, still delivers 518 kPa discharge, matching its commissioning curve.
Valve positions at the station are verified open, and the discharge header has no new fittings.
The duty pump motor current at test flow is slightly lower than at commissioning, not higher.
Zone pressures are maintained only because the standby pump now runs more hours than the duty pump.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The discharge logger is drifting low over the year
A partially closed discharge valve is throttling the duty pump
Suction supply to the station is deteriorating
The duty pump has lost head through internal wear, most likely worn wear rings increasing internal recirculation

inference.explanation: Suction is unchanged and valves are verified open. The standby pump on the same header and loggers holds its curve, which excludes logger drift and header problems and isolates the duty pump. Lower current with lower head fits internal recirculation, not throttling, which would change the operating point differently.

nextClue.prompt: Which test best confirms internal pump wear before overhaul?

options.label: Replace the discharge pressure logger
Open and close every station valve to free any obstruction
Run a full head versus flow test on the duty pump and compare it point by point with its commissioning curve

nextClue.explanation: A curve comparison quantifies head loss across flows and is the standard confirmation for wear. The standby comparison already cleared the logger, and valves are verified open.

clueText.nc-a: The standby pump reads correctly on the same logger, so the logger is not the fault.
clueText.nc-b: Station valves were verified open, so exercising them again does not test the pump.
clueText.nc-c: The duty pump curve sits 8 to 11 percent below commissioning at all flows, confirming uniform wear rather than a single point fault.

tasks.prompt: Two Ontario zones at different elevations were tied together for a summer construction project, and the tie was left in place after the project ended.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zones: Upper zone normal pressure 350 kPa at its low point, Lower zone normal 550 kPa at its high point. The construction tie connects them at mid elevation. Project ended four months ago.

evidence.label: Upper zone low streets now run at 480 kPa, with two plumbing damage claims since the project ended.
Lower zone high streets, formerly short of pressure at peak, now hold pressure unusually well.
The construction tie valve is found open, with its project tag still attached and no record of a permanent tie approval.
Closing the tie in a trial returns Upper low streets to 355 kPa and Lower pressures to their former pattern.
No pump or PRV settings were changed in either zone during or after the project.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The leftover open tie lets the Lower zone pressurise the Upper zone beyond its design range
Upper zone PRVs failed during the construction project
Upper zone demand fell, raising its pressures permanently
Lower zone pumps were uprated during the project

inference.explanation: No settings changed in either zone, and the trial closure restores both zones at once, which isolates the tie. The open valve with its project tag is the direct physical evidence.

nextClue.prompt: Which closeout control prevents leftover temporary ties?

options.label: Add temporary tie valves to the project closeout checklist with a signed closure verification and tag removal
Set both zones to the same pressure permanently
Remove the tie pipe entirely at the next capital project

nextClue.explanation: Checklist closure with verification catches temporary configurations while the project team is still engaged. Equalising zone pressures permanently would defeat the elevation based zone design.

clueText.nc-a: The checklist is adopted, and the next project closeout audit finds its temporary tie closed and verified.
clueText.nc-b: The zones exist because of a 200 kPa elevation driven difference; one pressure cannot serve both correctly.
clueText.nc-c: Removing pipe is costly and unnecessary; the fault was an unverified open valve, not the existence of a tie point.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario elevated tank shows a chlorine residual of 0.9 mg/L at its inlet but only 0.2 mg/L at nearby taps, and level records explain why.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional 2,500 m3 elevated tank floating on a zone with average day demand of 1,800 m3. Level is logged hourly. Inlet and outlet share one riser pipe.

evidence.label: Tank level varies only between 82 and 88 percent full over a typical week, a daily exchange of about 150 m3.
Zone demand is 1,800 m3 per day, but most of it passes the tank site through the grid without entering the tank.
Water entering the tank tests 0.9 mg/L free chlorine; water drawn from the tank outlet in a morning drain tests 0.25 mg/L.
A temperature profile shows the tank contents are stratified, with the oldest water at the top.
Neighbouring zones without storage hold 0.7 to 0.8 mg/L at their taps over the same week.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The tank inlet chlorine analyser over reads by 0.6 mg/L
The tank barely turns over, so stored water ages in place and loses residual before it reaches taps
Tank coating is consuming chlorine at the wall at a high rate
Zone demand is too low to supply the neighbourhood at all

inference.explanation: The level band proves only about 150 m3 exchanges daily in a 2,500 m3 tank, and outlet water drawn from storage is already at 0.25 mg/L, so ageing in storage is measured directly. Neighbouring zones hold residual, excluding a plant wide cause.

nextClue.prompt: Which operating change best restores turnover?

options.label: Raise the plant chlorine dose until tank taps reach target
Widen the tank operating level band so a much larger volume exchanges daily, within structural and pressure limits
Take the tank out of service permanently

nextClue.explanation: Increasing daily exchanged volume attacks the measured cause, water age. Raising plant dose treats every zone for one tank problem and still leaves old water in the tank.

clueText.nc-a: Higher plant dose would over chlorinate zones that already hold 0.7 to 0.8 mg/L.
clueText.nc-b: With the band widened to exchange about 900 m3 daily, tank outlet residual recovers to 0.65 mg/L within two weeks.
clueText.nc-c: Removing storage loses fire and peak capacity the zone was designed around.

tasks.prompt: Two identical Ontario ground reservoirs sit side by side. One holds residual well. The other loses residual and grows heterotrophic counts every summer.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional twin reservoirs, same age, same inlet water, same cleaning schedule. Each has a single inlet and outlet at opposite ends on Reservoir A, and adjacent at one corner on Reservoir B.

evidence.label: Reservoir A inlet residual is 0.85 mg/L and outlet residual is 0.70 mg/L in August sampling.
Reservoir B inlet residual is 0.86 mg/L but outlet residual is 0.30 mg/L in the same week.
A tracer style level and temperature study shows Reservoir B short circuits: inlet water reaches the outlet in hours while a corner pocket stays undisturbed for weeks.
Reservoir B inlet and outlet pipes are adjacent at one corner; Reservoir A pipes are at opposite ends.
Both reservoirs pass structural inspection and both were cleaned the same month.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Reservoir B has a leaking roof hatch admitting contamination
Reservoir B inlet water is lower in chlorine than Reservoir A inlet water
Reservoir B short circuits, so most stored water stagnates while a small stream passes quickly from inlet to outlet
Reservoir B is significantly older and its coating has failed

inference.explanation: Inlet residuals match, cleaning and inspection match, and age matches, excluding supply, contamination entry, and condition. The tracer study directly shows short circuiting with a stagnant pocket, which explains low outlet residual despite fresh inlet water.

nextClue.prompt: Which retrofit best fixes Reservoir B hydraulics?

options.label: Increase cleaning frequency for Reservoir B to monthly
Raise the inlet chlorine dose for Reservoir B only
Relocate or baffle the inlet or outlet so flow must traverse the reservoir, eliminating the short circuit path

nextClue.explanation: Fixing the flow path removes the stagnant pocket that cleaning and dosing cannot reach. Monthly cleaning is disruptive and the pocket reforms between cleans, and higher inlet dose still short circuits.

clueText.nc-a: Cleaning does not change the flow path, so the stagnant corner returns within weeks.
clueText.nc-b: Extra dose follows the short circuit to the outlet while the pocket water still ages.
clueText.nc-c: A baffle curtain is fitted, and the next August sampling shows Reservoir B outlet residual at 0.62 mg/L.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario standpipe zone reports taste complaints every spring, always in the first week the standpipe returns to full service after winter operation.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional standpipe operated at low level all winter to prevent freezing, then raised to full level in spring. Zone sampling runs year round.

evidence.label: Winter samples from the zone hold 0.6 mg/L residual with no taste complaints at the low operating level.
Each spring, within days of raising the level, residual at zone taps falls to 0.2 mg/L and taste complaints begin.
The raised level draws in a large volume that then sits: level records show the top third of the standpipe exchanges less than once per month.
Inlet water to the standpipe tests 0.9 mg/L through both winter and spring.
Neighbouring zones on the same supply report no spring taste or residual change.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Spring runoff degrades the source water for this zone only
The standpipe level transmitter fails each spring
Winter freezing damages the standpipe coating, releasing taste compounds
Raising the level creates a large stagnant top volume whose aged water degrades zone quality each spring

inference.explanation: Inlet water stays at 0.9 mg/L and neighbouring zones are unaffected, excluding source causes. Level records show the mechanism directly: the top third barely exchanges, so spring filling stores water that ages in place.

nextClue.prompt: Which spring operating practice best prevents the problem?

options.label: Raise the level in stages with deliberate drawdown cycles so new water mixes and exchanges instead of sitting
Keep the standpipe at winter level all year
Shock chlorinate the standpipe once each spring and then operate as before

nextClue.explanation: Staged filling with drawdown keeps the full volume exchanging. A single shock dose decays in the same stagnant volume, and staying at winter level sacrifices needed storage.

clueText.nc-a: Staged spring filling holds zone residual above 0.55 mg/L with no taste complaints that season.
clueText.nc-b: Year round low level removes the peak and fire storage the standpipe provides in summer.
clueText.nc-c: One shock dose does not change the exchange rate, so residual falls again as the water ages.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario reservoir outlet samples fail for total coliform once, while inlet samples and all zone samples pass, and the reservoir was entered for inspection two weeks earlier.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional ground reservoir returned to service after an internal inspection. Ontario Regulation 170/03 sampling applies. Disinfection and sampling records for the return to service are on file.

evidence.label: The reservoir was drained, inspected, and refilled; the return to service record shows disinfection was shortened because of a schedule overrun.
Inlet samples before and after the event pass, with residual at 0.8 mg/L.
The single outlet failure is followed by three consecutive passing outlet samples over the next week with no further intervention beyond normal operation.
Zone samples downstream pass throughout, and no customer illness reports are received.
A hatch seal on the reservoir roof is found intact, and the vent screen is undamaged.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The shortened return to service disinfection most likely left residual contamination that normal turnover then flushed out
The reservoir has an ongoing contamination entry through its roof
The inlet supply became contaminated for one day
The laboratory produced a false positive and no event occurred

inference.explanation: Roof and vent are intact and inlet samples pass, excluding ongoing entry and supply causes. A one time failure that clears with turnover, right after a documented shortened disinfection, fits a return to service lapse. A lab error is possible in general but the record gives a concrete procedural cause that must be addressed regardless.

nextClue.prompt: Which corrective action best addresses the procedural cause?

options.label: Close the reservoir permanently
Make the full return to service disinfection and clearance sampling a hold point that cannot be shortened for schedule reasons
Increase routine outlet sampling to daily for a year

nextClue.explanation: The failure mode is procedural, so the control must be procedural. Daily sampling detects but does not prevent, and closure removes needed storage for a correctable process fault.

clueText.nc-a: Closure is disproportionate when the cause is a shortened procedure that can be enforced.
clueText.nc-b: The hold point is added to the procedure, and the next two reservoir returns complete full disinfection with passing clearance samples.
clueText.nc-c: Daily sampling for a year consumes laboratory capacity while leaving the shortened disinfection risk in place.

tasks.prompt: Level data for an Ontario tank shows it fills every night and drains every day, yet water quality at its outlet keeps worsening month by month.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional tank with separate inlet at the bottom and outlet at the bottom on opposite sides, no mixer, strong summer stratification measured by a temperature chain.

evidence.label: Daily level swing is 25 percent of tank volume, showing regular fill and drain cycles.
Temperature chain shows a warm top layer 6 C above the bottom layer through the summer.
Outlet samples, drawn from the bottom, test well, but a sample from the top access hatch tests 0.05 mg/L residual with high heterotrophic counts.
Dye added at the inlet during filling stays in the bottom layer and exits within a day, barely mixing upward.
Inlet residual is steady at 0.9 mg/L and the tank was cleaned last year.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The tank level swing is too small to exchange any water
The tank cycles its bottom layer only: thermal stratification prevents mixing, so the top layer ages indefinitely despite daily level swings
The outlet sampling tap is contaminated and gives false results
The inlet chlorine decays instantly on entering the tank

inference.explanation: A 25 percent daily swing is substantial exchange, but the dye study shows it is confined to the bottom layer. Top hatch sampling proves the aged layer exists. Outlet samples test well precisely because they draw the fresh bottom layer, which is why the problem hid.

nextClue.prompt: Which fix best addresses the hidden aged layer?

options.label: Increase the daily level swing to 40 percent
Move the routine sampling point to the top hatch
Install or restore active mixing in the tank and verify with a post mixing temperature and residual profile

nextClue.explanation: Mixing destroys the stratification that isolates the top layer. A larger swing still cycles mainly the bottom, and moving the sample point measures the problem without fixing it.

clueText.nc-a: A bigger swing exchanges more bottom water while the stratified top layer remains isolated.
clueText.nc-b: Sampling the top documents poor quality but leaves aged water to be drawn down in a high demand event.
clueText.nc-c: After mixer installation, top and bottom residuals agree within 0.1 mg/L and the temperature profile is uniform.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario utility finds one tank consistently 5 years into a paint failure and sediment problem while its twin tank on the same site is clean.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional twin tanks, same construction year and coating system. Drain down inspection records and sediment depths are kept for both. One tank sits under large trees; the other is in the open.

evidence.label: Tank South sediment depth at inspection is 30 mm, with coating blistering concentrated near the roof edge.
Tank North sediment depth is 3 mm and its coating is sound at the same inspection interval.
Tank South roof vent screen is torn, and leaf litter and insects are found inside the roof edge gutter area.
Both tanks receive the same inlet water, turnover, and cleaning contractor.
Tank South overflow pipe screen is also damaged, while Tank North screens are intact.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Tank South receives more corrosive water than Tank North
The cleaning contractor cleans Tank South less thoroughly on purpose
Debris and organisms entering through Tank South damaged screens drive its sediment and coating deterioration
Tank South coating was applied thinner at construction

inference.explanation: Both tanks share inlet water, turnover, and contractor, excluding supply and service causes. The torn vent and overflow screens on South alone, with debris found inside, give a direct entry path that North does not have.

nextClue.prompt: Which inspection program change follows?

options.label: Add screen and vent integrity checks to the routine external tank inspection, with repair before the next drain down
Recoat Tank South on a shorter cycle than Tank North
Sample Tank South inlet water weekly for corrosivity

nextClue.explanation: Screen checks catch the entry path cheaply and early. Recoating more often treats damage without stopping entry, and inlet sampling cannot differ between tanks sharing one supply.

clueText.nc-a: Screens are added to the external checklist, and the next inspection finds and repairs a new vent tear before debris enters.
clueText.nc-b: Shorter recoating cycles cost heavily while torn screens keep admitting debris.
clueText.nc-c: Shared inlet water cannot explain a one tank difference, so weekly sampling adds no diagnostic value.

tasks.prompt: A small Ontario system keeps its only reservoir nearly full at all times for security of supply, and its distribution residuals keep failing in summer.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional single reservoir system, reservoir volume equals 4 days of average demand. Operators hold level between 95 and 100 percent. Summer water temperature reaches 22 C.

evidence.label: Reservoir level stays between 95 and 100 percent, exchanging about 5 percent of volume per day.
Distribution residuals fall from 0.8 mg/L at the reservoir inlet to below 0.2 mg/L at far taps each July and August.
Winter residuals at the same taps hold above 0.5 mg/L at the same operating levels.
A drawdown test week, operating between 60 and 95 percent, restores far tap residuals to 0.55 mg/L in July.
No nitrification indicators are present: the system uses free chlorine, and ammonia and nitrite are both near zero.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Nitrification in the reservoir is consuming the chlorine
The reservoir is leaking treated water and drawing in groundwater
Summer demand exceeds the reservoir capacity
Very low turnover gives summer water several days of age in the reservoir, and warm temperatures complete the residual loss

inference.explanation: Ammonia and nitrite near zero in a free chlorine system exclude nitrification. The drawdown test at the same summer temperatures restores residual by turnover alone, proving water age, not leakage or capacity, is the driver.

nextClue.prompt: Which operating policy best balances supply security and quality here?

options.label: Keep the reservoir at 95 to 100 percent and raise the plant dose in summer
Adopt a seasonal operating band that guarantees a minimum daily exchange while keeping a defined emergency reserve volume
Empty and refill the reservoir completely every week

nextClue.explanation: A defined band with a protected reserve quantifies both needs instead of trading one for the other. Raising dose leaves multi day old water in place, and weekly full cycling wastes water and stresses the structure.

clueText.nc-a: Higher dose into 4 day old warm water still decays before the far taps and raises by product concerns.
clueText.nc-b: The seasonal band holds far tap residuals above 0.5 mg/L through August while the reserve volume stays untouched.
clueText.nc-c: Weekly complete emptying discards treated water and leaves the system with no reserve during the refill.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario tank fills from the bottom through the same pipe it drains from, and first draw water each morning is always the poorest quality of the day.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional common inlet outlet riser tank. Morning first draw is sampled at a tap near the tank before any other zone demand. Fill occurs overnight.

evidence.label: First draw samples at 06:00 test 0.15 mg/L residual, while midday samples at the same tap test 0.70 mg/L.
Overnight fill enters through the riser and the tank drains through the same riser from 06:00 onward.
A residual profile sampled through the riser during drain shows quality improving steadily as draining continues.
Tank total volume exchanges about 40 percent daily, and inlet residual is 0.9 mg/L.
No other zone on the system shows a morning quality dip.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The riser delivers the oldest water first: water that sat in the riser and tank bottom overnight leaves before fresher water
The plant chlorine dose dips every night at the same time
The morning sampling tap has a contaminated aerator
Zone demand each morning flushes sediment into the tap

inference.explanation: Plant dose is steady and no other zone dips, excluding a plant cause. The improving profile during drain is the signature of oldest first delivery through a common riser, and it repeats daily on a schedule a tap fault would not produce across the profile samples.

nextClue.prompt: Which design or operating response fits a common riser pattern?

options.label: Replace the sampling tap aerator and resample
Raise the overnight fill pressure to push fresher water deeper
Evaluate a separate inlet, a riser mixer, or a scheduled small night draw to clear riser water before the morning peak

nextClue.explanation: Each listed option attacks riser stagnation directly. The aerator cannot explain a whole drain profile, and fill pressure does not change which water leaves first.

clueText.nc-a: The drain profile samples came from the riser stream, not just the tap, so the tap is not the source.
clueText.nc-b: Fill pressure changes how fast the tank fills, not the oldest first order of delivery.
clueText.nc-c: A small programmed night draw clears the riser, and first draw residual rises to 0.55 mg/L the following week.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario reservoir shows rising water age calculations even though its level cycles normally, after a new subdivision connects to its zone.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional reservoir zone. A new subdivision was connected with its own new ground tank that floats on the same zone. Combined storage is now double the original design for current demand.

evidence.label: Zone demand grew only 10 percent with the subdivision, while total floating storage grew 100 percent.
Calculated average water age in the zone rose from 2 days to 5 days in the year after connection.
Residuals at zone extremities fell steadily over the same year, with no change in plant dose.
Level records show both tanks cycling shallowly in parallel, each exchanging about 15 percent daily.
No new dead ends were created, and flushing records for the zone are unchanged.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The new subdivision mains are leaking chlorine demanding water
Doubling storage for a 10 percent demand increase diluted turnover across both tanks, raising system water age
Plant dose fell without being recorded
The new tank coating consumes chlorine heavily

inference.explanation: Both tanks cycle shallowly in parallel, which is the arithmetic of doubled storage on near flat demand. Plant dose is recorded steady, and a coating effect in one tank would not raise calculated age zone wide or shallow the old tank cycling.

nextClue.prompt: Which coordination measure best restores age targets?

options.label: Operate the two tanks in a coordinated cycle, drawing one down while the other rests, to restore effective turnover
Raise the plant dose to offset the age increase
Flush zone extremities weekly to pull fresher water through

nextClue.explanation: Coordinated cycling restores exchange per tank without new infrastructure. Dose increases and flushing treat symptoms at extremities while the storage volume still turns over slowly.

clueText.nc-a: Coordinated cycling brings average age back to about 2.5 days and extremity residuals recover within a month.
clueText.nc-b: Higher dose decays over 5 days of age and does not restore turnover.
clueText.nc-c: Weekly flushing wastes treated water and only freshens the flushed paths temporarily.

tasks.prompt: Taste and odour complaints cluster in one Ontario tank zone every fall for about two weeks, then stop on their own.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone served by a ground reservoir near a deciduous treeline. Complaints are earthy taste reports. The reservoir has a floating cover in good condition and screened vents.

evidence.label: Complaints begin within days of peak fall leaf drop and end about two weeks later, three years in a row.
Reservoir inlet samples, taken from the plant clearwell supply, show no taste compounds and normal residuals.
A sample from the reservoir outlet during the complaint window carries the earthy taste, while inlet samples the same day do not.
Roof inspection finds leaf debris ponded against a low roof drain, and the drain discharges near an unscreened overflow opening with a damaged flap.
Zones without storage on the same supply report no fall taste complaints.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The source water develops earthy taste every fall for all zones
The reservoir liner releases taste compounds in cold weather
Leaf debris at the damaged overflow flap is contaminating the reservoir surface during the fall window
Fall chlorination changes at the plant cause the taste

inference.explanation: Inlet samples are clean on complaint days and storage free zones are unaffected, excluding source and plant causes. Outlet only taste plus a found entry path with ponded leaf debris localises the fault to the reservoir roof and overflow.

nextClue.prompt: Which preventive action best fits the seasonal pattern?

options.label: Change the plant taste treatment process each fall
Repair the overflow flap and add a pre fall roof and drain inspection to the seasonal maintenance list
Keep the reservoir out of service every fall

nextClue.explanation: Repair plus seasonal inspection targets the entry path at the time of year it matters. Plant changes cannot help when inlet water is already clean, and seasonal removal loses storage.

clueText.nc-a: Inlet samples prove plant water is clean during the window, so plant treatment is not the fault.
clueText.nc-b: With the flap repaired and roof drains cleared each September, the next fall passes with no taste complaints in the zone.
clueText.nc-c: Removing the reservoir each fall sacrifices storage for a repairable flap and a cleaning task.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario tank zone passes residual tests at the tank outlet but fails at a school 800 m away, only during school holidays.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone. The school is the largest user on a short branch main off the tank feed. During term the school draws heavily on weekdays. Holiday sampling is done on the same weekday schedule.

evidence.label: Tank outlet residual holds 0.75 mg/L year round.
School tap residual is 0.65 mg/L during term and falls below 0.2 mg/L after two weeks of holidays, recovering within days of reopening.
Homes before the school branch hold 0.6 mg/L in both periods.
The school branch main is 300 m of 150 mm pipe that sees almost no flow while the school is closed.
A holiday flush of the branch at the school hydrant restores school tap residual to 0.6 mg/L the same day.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The tank loses residual during school holidays
The school plumbing consumes chlorine only when the building is empty
Holiday sampling is done with faulty test kits
Water stagnates in the school branch during closures, so the failure is local branch age, not tank or zone quality

inference.explanation: Tank outlet and upstream homes hold residual in both periods, excluding tank and zone causes. The branch flush restoring residual the same day proves the aged water sits in the branch itself.

nextClue.prompt: Which program step best manages this predictable pattern?

options.label: Increase tank outlet residual targets year round
Replace the school internal plumbing
Add the school branch to the scheduled flushing list for closure periods longer than one week

nextClue.explanation: Scheduled branch flushing during closures matches the predictable stagnation window. Higher tank targets expose the whole zone to more chlorine for a 300 m branch problem, and internal plumbing is downstream of the sampled tap pattern that flushing already fixes.

clueText.nc-a: Tank outlet water is already 0.75 mg/L; the loss occurs in the stagnant branch, not in storage.
clueText.nc-b: Flushing at the hydrant restored the tap result, showing the branch main, not building plumbing, holds the aged water.
clueText.nc-c: Holiday flushing holds school tap residual above 0.55 mg/L through the next summer closure.

tasks.prompt: After an Ontario reservoir is returned from a summer out of service, its zone shows the best residuals in the system for a month, then declines to the worst.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional reservoir cleaned and disinfected during a 6 week outage, then returned. Zone residual trending is monthly. Operating levels before and after the outage are set by the same SCADA program.

evidence.label: During the first month back, zone residuals average 0.8 mg/L, the system best.
By month three, zone residuals average 0.3 mg/L, the system worst, with no change in plant dose.
SCADA level history shows the reservoir operating band creeping upward month by month as operators top it up after each high demand day.
By month three the band sits between 90 and 97 percent, exchanging about 8 percent daily, against 35 percent daily in month one.
No coating work, source change, or main work occurred in the zone during the decline.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Operator top up habits shrank the operating band after return to service, so turnover decayed and residuals followed
The cleaning chemicals damaged the reservoir coating, causing delayed chlorine demand
A new chlorine demanding deposit formed in zone mains over three months
The plant dose declined gradually without alarming

inference.explanation: Plant dose is recorded steady and no zone work occurred. The level history gives a complete mechanism: exchange fell from 35 to 8 percent daily as the band crept up, tracking the residual decline month by month.

nextClue.prompt: Which SCADA control prevents band creep?

options.label: Lock the operating band in SCADA with an alarm on any manual level setpoint change, reviewed weekly
Schedule reservoir cleaning every three months
Raise the plant dose each month to match the decline

nextClue.explanation: Alarming setpoint changes protects turnover automatically. Quarterly cleaning is costly and disruptive for an operating practice fault, and chasing dose treats the symptom while age keeps rising.

clueText.nc-a: With the band locked at the design range, daily exchange holds near 35 percent and zone residuals stabilise at 0.7 mg/L.
clueText.nc-b: Cleaning restored quality only while turnover was high; the decline followed the band, not the cleaning date.
clueText.nc-c: Dose increases cannot offset water that sits for many days, and they raise costs system wide.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario elevated tank ice problem: each winter the tank develops internal ice that damages the riser, and operators respond by keeping the tank as full as possible.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional elevated tank in a cold climate zone. Winter level strategy has been to hold the tank near full to reduce ice movement. Riser repairs were needed in two of the last four winters.

evidence.label: Ice forms on the tank walls each winter and the riser has cracked twice at the same elevation band.
Level records show the tank held between 92 and 100 percent all winter, so the ice sheet barely moves vertically.
A sister tank in the next town, operated with a wide daily level swing, has had no riser ice damage in ten winters.
Water temperature entering both tanks in winter is about 4 C, and both tanks are uninsulated steel of similar age.
The riser cracks sit at the elevation where the static ice sheet edge bears on the riser during brief drawdowns.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The riser steel is defective and cracks at random elevations
Holding the tank full keeps a static ice sheet grinding at one riser elevation; regular level movement is protective, not harmful
Inlet water is colder in this town than in the sister town
The tank needs to be kept even fuller to stop all ice formation

inference.explanation: Cracks repeat at one elevation band, not random points, and inlet temperatures match the undamaged sister tank. The sister tank wide swing record shows movement prevents the damaging static sheet, the opposite of the current strategy.

nextClue.prompt: Which winter operating change best fits the evidence?

options.label: Keep the tank at 100 percent and heat trace the riser only
Operate the tank with a deliberate daily level swing through winter, within pressure and reserve limits, to keep ice from fixing at one elevation
Drain the tank completely each winter

nextClue.explanation: Daily movement addresses the mechanism shown by the sister tank comparison. Heat tracing one riser section leaves the static sheet bearing elsewhere, and full drainage removes winter storage entirely.

clueText.nc-a: Heat tracing treats one spot while the static sheet still bears on unheated elevations during drawdowns.
clueText.nc-b: With a daily winter swing in place, the next two winters pass with no new riser damage.
clueText.nc-c: Draining removes fire and peak storage for the whole winter season.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario reservoir level falls 0.4 m overnight with all outlets closed and no demand, twice in one month, then holds normally for weeks.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional ground reservoir with level logging, a valved outlet, an overflow to a storm pond, and a floor drain to a sump with a flow switch. Nights in question had no zone demand on the reservoir.

evidence.label: Level falls 0.4 m over 6 hours on two nights, equal to about 180 m3, with the outlet valve confirmed closed.
The sump flow switch logged flow on both nights and was dry on normal nights.
The reservoir floor drain valve was operated for a cleaning contractor visit the day before the first loss night.
When the floor drain valve is exercised and reseated under supervision, the level holds steady the following three nights.
No overflow was recorded at the storm pond, and the reservoir passed a structural level test the previous year.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The reservoir floor has developed an intermittent crack
Groundwater pressure lifts and reseals a floor joint at night
The floor drain valve was left slightly open after the contractor visit and later reseated, explaining the intermittent losses
The level transmitter drops 0.4 m on cold nights

inference.explanation: Loss nights match sump flow logging, tying the loss to the drain path, not the structure or the instrument. Reseating the drain valve stops the loss, and a crack would not respond to valve exercise or align with the contractor visit.

nextClue.prompt: Which closeout step prevents a repeat after contractor work?

options.label: Pressure test the reservoir floor annually
Replace the level transmitter
Require a post work valve position verification and an overnight level watch sign off after any reservoir drain operation

nextClue.explanation: Verification after drain work catches a valve left cracked open while correction is trivial. The transmitter agreed with the sump evidence, and annual floor testing does not address valve operation.

clueText.nc-a: The sump log already proved the water left by the drain, so floor testing investigates the wrong path.
clueText.nc-b: Level loss was real water movement confirmed by sump flow, not an instrument artefact.
clueText.nc-c: The sign off is added, and the next contractor visit closes with a verified shut drain and a steady overnight level.

tasks.prompt: Water quality in an Ontario tank zone improves measurably in the year after the utility paints the tank, and the improvement is credited to the new coating.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional tank recoated inside and out. During the painting outage, a failed inlet check valve at the tank was also replaced, a fact recorded only in the outage work orders. Residual trending spans two years.

evidence.label: Zone residuals rose from an average 0.35 mg/L before the outage to 0.70 mg/L after, sustained for a year.
The old inlet check valve was found stuck half open, letting tank water slosh back into the feed main and refill repeatedly.
With the stuck check, the same water could enter and leave the tank zone many times, raising effective age near the tank.
A neighbouring tank recoated the same year, with a sound check valve, showed no residual change after painting.
Tank turnover volumes and plant dose were unchanged across the outage.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Interior coating always doubles zone residuals for a year
The painting outage flushed the zone mains and the effect lasted a year
Operators paid more attention to the zone after the capital project
The improvement came from replacing the stuck check valve that was recirculating aged water, not from the new coating

inference.explanation: The recoated neighbour tank with a sound check valve showed no improvement, which breaks the coating explanation. The stuck check gives a physical recirculation mechanism, and its replacement is the one functional change that matches the sustained gain.

nextClue.prompt: Which lesson should be recorded for future tank outages?

options.label: Include check valve and appurtenance function tests in every tank outage scope, since outage work can hide the real cause of quality changes
Credit coating projects with water quality benefits in future business cases
Recoat tanks more frequently to maintain the residual gain

nextClue.explanation: Recording the appurtenance lesson preserves the true mechanism for future planning. Crediting coating would misdirect capital toward paint when a valve test is the effective action.

clueText.nc-a: The outage scope template now includes check valve testing, and the next tank outage finds and replaces a second failing check.
clueText.nc-b: The neighbour tank comparison shows coating alone produced no residual gain.
clueText.nc-c: More frequent recoating is major capital spending aimed at an effect the evidence assigns to a valve.

tasks.prompt: An Ontario system with two tanks in one zone finds total chlorine adequate leaving the plant, but one tank zone extremity repeatedly tests low in late summer.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional free chlorine system. Tank A is near the plant. Tank B is at the far end of the zone on a long single feed. Summer sampling covers both tank outlets and the extremity beyond Tank B.

evidence.label: Plant outlet residual is 1.0 mg/L all summer.
Tank A outlet tests 0.85 mg/L and its zone taps pass.
Tank B outlet tests 0.45 mg/L, and the extremity beyond it tests 0.15 mg/L in late summer.
Tank B level cycles only 10 percent daily: its feed is long and the zone beyond it is small, so exchange is slow.
Tank B inlet, sampled during filling, tests 0.80 mg/L.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Tank B slow turnover ages its water, and the extremity beyond it receives the oldest water in the system
Tank A is consuming the chlorine before water reaches Tank B
The extremity sampling station is faulty in summer only
Tank B coating is highly chlorine demanding

inference.explanation: Tank B inlet during filling is 0.80 mg/L, so water arrives with residual intact, excluding upstream consumption. Its outlet at 0.45 after slow cycling, and the extremity lower still, trace the loss to age in and beyond Tank B.

nextClue.prompt: Which targeted action best helps the extremity?

options.label: Raise the plant dose until the extremity passes
Increase Tank B turnover with a revised level band and consider a small rechlorination point at Tank B outlet if residuals still fall short
Replace the extremity sampling station

nextClue.explanation: Turnover at Tank B plus local rechlorination treats the oldest water where it is. Raising plant dose over chlorinates Tank A zone, which already passes, and the sampling station agrees with the Tank B outlet trend.

clueText.nc-a: Plant dose is already 1.0 mg/L with Tank A at 0.85; the loss is age beyond Tank B, not dose.
clueText.nc-b: A wider Tank B band lifts its outlet to 0.65 mg/L and the extremity to 0.40 mg/L through late summer.
clueText.nc-c: The station trend matches Tank B outlet values, so the station is reporting the water correctly.

tasks.prompt: A chloraminated Ontario system watches total chlorine fall across one storage tank each August, with nitrite appearing at the outlet.
